The agent acts as a Technical Implementation Partner and TDD Coach - providing guidance, generating test cases and implementation code that follows existing patterns, avoids over-engineering, and produces idiomatic, modern code in the target language.

It automatically detects the input type and creates properly formatted code task files following the code task format specification. For PDD plans, it processes implementation steps one at a time to allow for learning and adaptation between steps. For shaping packages, it generates an implementation plan from the shaped design and then produces tasks from the approved plan. When the work involves scaffolding a new project, it emits a dedicated scaffold task that uses the `intropy` CLI to generate the project skeleton before any implementation begins.

Use for any task involving Intropy concepts: blocks (Extractor, Loader, Reconciler, Assembler), blueprints (Golden Record, Product Sync, Order Import), archetypes (Pub/Sub, Aggregator, API Service), connectors, or the Intropy model. The process is designed to be iterative, allowing movement between requirements clarification and research as needed.
- pipeline-runs: Query pipeline execution runs for a given integration tag. Looks up services in the Backstage catalog by tag, then queries Tempo for matching pipeline traces. Use this skill when someone asks to "show runs", "list executions", "find pipeline traces", or "check pipeline activity" for an integration identifier like "int201", "int305", etc. Also trigger when the user mentions "runs for <tag>", "pipeline runs", "trace search for integration", or wants to see what happened for a specific integration over a time range.

Use this skill whenever someone asks to add a new infrastructure component, deploy a new Helm chart to the service plane, set up a new platform service, onboard a new operator or tool to the cluster, or scaffold GitOps manifests for a service. - chrome-devtools-mcp:chrome-devtools: Uses Chrome DevTools via MCP for efficient debugging, troubleshooting and browser automation. - chrome-devtools-mcp:chrome-devtools-cli: Use this skill to write shell scripts or run shell commands to automate tasks in the browser or otherwise use Chrome DevTools via CLI.
- chrome-devtools-mcp:debug-optimize-lcp: Guides debugging and optimizing Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) using Chrome DevTools MCP tools. - chrome-devtools-mcp:troubleshooting: Uses Chrome DevTools MCP and documentation to troubleshoot connection and target issues. Trigger this skill when list_pages, new_page, or navigate_page fail, or when the server initialization fails.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Run before committing nontrivial changes. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

# Agent Instructions

This project is a .NET transactional integration job built on the Intropy
framework. It reads files from a local Dapr file binding, publishes each one
onto an in-memory Dapr pub/sub topic, and processes them through a VETER send
pipeline that writes the transformed result to a second local file binding.

## Project overview

- Framework: .NET 10
- App type: Console job (no web endpoints)
- Runner: `Intropy.Framework.Hosting.TransactionalIntegration.Job.TransactionalIntegrationRunner`
- Pub/sub component: `pubsub` (in-memory)
- Topic: `orders`
- Source binding: `inbound-storage` (Dapr local storage, rootPath `/tmp/{{ .name | kebabcase }}/inbound`)
- Destination binding: `outbound-storage` (Dapr local storage, rootPath `/tmp/{{ .name | kebabcase }}/outbound`)

## Important files

- `src/Program.cs` - DI wiring and entrypoint that runs the `TransactionalIntegrationRunner`.
- `src/Configuration/Constants.cs` - component names, keyed-adapter keys, context metadata keys.
- `src/Receive/` - source listing and the receive pipeline steps (`Receiver`, `Enqueuer`, `Completer`).
- `src/Send/` - the VETER send pipeline steps.
- `local/dapr-components/pubsub.yaml` - in-memory pub/sub component.
- `local/dapr-components/inbound-storage.yaml` / `outbound-storage.yaml` - Dapr local storage bindings.
- `local/sample-data/sample-order.json` - sample input to drop into the inbound folder.

## Development notes

- Source and destination `IFileAdapter` instances are registered as keyed singletons
  (`Constants.SourceFileAdapterKey`, `Constants.DestinationFileAdapterKey`). Inject them
  via `[FromKeyedServices(...)]` or resolve via `GetRequiredKeyedService<IFileAdapter>(...)`.
- The receive pipeline runs once per file returned by `ISourceLister`; the send
  pipeline runs once per pub/sub delivery.
- Keep `Constants.PubSubName` / `Constants.TopicName` in sync between
  `Program.cs` (`AddTransactionalIntegration`) and the Dapr component YAML.
- The send pipeline does not use idempotency or business-incident services in this
  sample - it is deliberately minimal. Add `.WithIdempotency(...)` and
  `.WithBusinessIncidents(...)` to the builder in `Send/ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs`
  once those services are reachable.

- **CLI** (`intropy-cli`): no code reads `intropy.yaml`. The only blueprint manifest the CLI knows is `template.yaml`. Five other skills (`intropy-getting-started`, `intropy-dapr`, `intropy-code-review`, `intropy-pipeline`, `intropy-endpoint`) mention it as the place to find the run command.

# Intropy component manifests

Every Intropy integration component carries two project-level manifest files at its root: `intropy.yaml`, which tells the `intropy` CLI how to start the component under Dapr, and `agent.md`, a terse project guide for agents working in the repo. This skill covers both, plus the canonical directory layout they describe.

## Project shape

A scaffolded component looks like this:

```
<component>/
├── agent.md                     # agent-facing project guide
├── intropy.yaml                 # run manifest (dapr ports, command)
├── README.md
├── local/
│   └── dapr-components/         # local Dapr component YAMLs (pub/sub, bindings)
└── src/
    ├── Program.cs               # DI wiring + framework registration
    ├── <Component>.csproj
    ├── appsettings*.json
    ├── Configuration/
    │   └── Constants.cs         # component/topic/binding/customer names
    ├── Ingest/
    │   └── Endpoints.cs         # MapPost + .WithTopic + StepResult → response
    ├── Model/                   # in/out records
    └── Process/
        ├── <Entity>SendPipeline.cs            # implements ISendPipeline<Context>
        ├── <Entity>SendPipelineBuilder.cs     # fluent builder
        ├── ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs     # AddXxxSendPipeline()
        └── Steps/                             # one file per Block subclass
```

When in doubt about where new code belongs, match this layout. Don't introduce parallel folders or rename existing ones — other tooling (and the scaffolder blueprint) rely on these paths.

## `intropy.yaml` — the run manifest

The CLI uses `intropy.yaml` to know how to start the component under Dapr. The today-shape:

```yaml
apiVersion: intropy.dev/v1
kind: Integration
metadata:
  name: HelloWorld
spec:
  run:
    appId: HelloWorld
    appPort: 5001
    daprHttpPort: 3500
    resourcesPath: ./local/dapr-components
    command:
      - dotnet
      - run
      - --project
      - ./src
      - --urls
      - http://localhost:{{ .AppPort }}
```

What's load-bearing:

- **`appId`** must match `Constants.ComponentName` (which is also what gets passed to `AddIntropyFramework(x => x.ComponentName = ...)`). It's the identity Dapr uses for the sidecar.
- **`resourcesPath`** points at the directory of Dapr component YAMLs. Keep it relative to the component root and in sync with the actual on-disk path.
- **`command`** is templated with `{{ .AppPort }}` so the CLI can substitute a free port when needed. If you add another templated value (e.g. `{{ .DaprHttpPort }}`), use the same Go-template syntax.
- **`appPort`** must match the `--urls` port in the command. If you change one, change the other.

If you add a new Dapr component, you generally **don't** need to touch `intropy.yaml` — the sidecar discovers everything in `resourcesPath`. You update `intropy.yaml` only when the *run shape* changes (port, command, app id). The component YAMLs themselves are covered by `intropy-dapr`.

## `agent.md` — the agent-facing project guide

`agent.md` is the project's guide for agents — package names, key files, run command. Keep it terse and concrete: bullet points, no prose essays.

Update it whenever the facts it states change, so the next agent invocation has accurate context:

- Added a state store, a binding, or a second pub/sub under `local/dapr-components/`.
- Renamed a topic or component (bump `Constants.cs` and the Dapr YAML in the same change).
- Changed the run command or ports.

## What to avoid

- **Don't let `appId` and `Constants.ComponentName` drift.** The mismatch is silent at compile time and shows up as Dapr identity confusion at runtime. Change both in the same commit.
- **Don't point `resourcesPath` at a path that doesn't exist** — the sidecar starts with no components and messages disappear into the void.
- **Don't let `agent.md` go stale.** A wrong run command or missing component listing misleads every future agent session in the repo.

- The run command in `intropy.yaml` starts the component under Dapr — run it from the component root and confirm the app comes up on `appPort` and the sidecar loads the components from `resourcesPath`.
- Confirm `spec.run.appId` matches `Constants.ComponentName` in `src/Configuration/Constants.cs`.
- Skim `agent.md` and check that its run command, ports, and component listing match `intropy.yaml` and `local/dapr-components/`.

# Intropy component manifests

Every Intropy integration component carries two project-level manifest files at its root: `intropy.yaml`, which tells the `intropy` CLI how to start the component under Dapr, and `agent.md`, a terse project guide for agents working in the repo. This skill covers both, plus the canonical directory layout they describe.

## Project shape

A scaffolded component looks like this:

```
<component>/
├── agent.md                     # agent-facing project guide
├── intropy.yaml                 # run manifest (dapr ports, command)
├── README.md
├── local/
│   └── dapr-components/         # local Dapr component YAMLs (pub/sub, bindings)
└── src/
    ├── Program.cs               # DI wiring + framework registration
    ├── <Component>.csproj
    ├── appsettings*.json
    ├── Configuration/
    │   └── Constants.cs         # component/topic/binding/customer names
    ├── Ingest/
    │   └── Endpoints.cs         # MapPost + .WithTopic + StepResult → response
    ├── Model/                   # in/out records
    └── Process/
        ├── <Entity>SendPipeline.cs            # implements ISendPipeline<Context>
        ├── <Entity>SendPipelineBuilder.cs     # fluent builder
        ├── ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs     # AddXxxSendPipeline()
        └── Steps/                             # one file per Block subclass
```

When in doubt about where new code belongs, match this layout. Don't introduce parallel folders or rename existing ones — other tooling (and the scaffolder blueprint) rely on these paths.

## `intropy.yaml` — the run manifest

The CLI uses `intropy.yaml` to know how to start the component under Dapr. The today-shape:

```yaml
apiVersion: intropy.dev/v1
kind: Integration
metadata:
  name: HelloWorld
spec:
  run:
    appId: HelloWorld
    appPort: 5001
    daprHttpPort: 3500
    resourcesPath: ./local/dapr-components
    command:
      - dotnet
      - run
      - --project
      - ./src
      - --urls
      - http://localhost:{{ .AppPort }}
```

What's load-bearing:

- **`appId`** must match `Constants.ComponentName` (which is also what gets passed to `AddIntropyFramework(x => x.ComponentName = ...)`). It's the identity Dapr uses for the sidecar.
- **`resourcesPath`** points at the directory of Dapr component YAMLs. Keep it relative to the component root and in sync with the actual on-disk path.
- **`command`** is templated with `{{ .AppPort }}` so the CLI can substitute a free port when needed. If you add another templated value (e.g. `{{ .DaprHttpPort }}`), use the same Go-template syntax.
- **`appPort`** must match the `--urls` port in the command. If you change one, change the other.

If you add a new Dapr component, you generally **don't** need to touch `intropy.yaml` — the sidecar discovers everything in `resourcesPath`. You update `intropy.yaml` only when the *run shape* changes (port, command, app id). The component YAMLs themselves are covered by `intropy-dapr`.

## `agent.md` — the agent-facing project guide

`agent.md` is the project's guide for agents — package names, key files, run command. Keep it terse and concrete: bullet points, no prose essays.

Update it whenever the facts it states change, so the next agent invocation has accurate context:

- Added a state store, a binding, or a second pub/sub under `local/dapr-components/`.
- Renamed a topic or component (bump `Constants.cs` and the Dapr YAML in the same change).
- Changed the run command or ports.

## What to avoid

- **Don't let `appId` and `Constants.ComponentName` drift.** The mismatch is silent at compile time and shows up as Dapr identity confusion at runtime. Change both in the same commit.
- **Don't point `resourcesPath` at a path that doesn't exist** — the sidecar starts with no components and messages disappear into the void.
- **Don't let `agent.md` go stale.** A wrong run command or missing component listing misleads every future agent session in the repo.

## Verification

- The run command in `intropy.yaml` starts the component under Dapr — run it from the component root and confirm the app comes up on `appPort` and the sidecar loads the components from `resourcesPath`.
- Confirm `spec.run.appId` matches `Constants.ComponentName` in `src/Configuration/Constants.cs`.
- Skim `agent.md` and check that its run command, ports, and component listing match `intropy.yaml` and `local/dapr-components/`.

An **Intropy blueprint** is a scaffold-style template: a manifest (`template.yaml`) declaring parameters, plus a skeleton file tree. The `intropy` CLI renders a blueprint plus your parameter values into a working project. Blueprints are fetched by release tag from the blueprint library, so the same inputs always produce the same output.

## Prerequisites

- **.NET 10 SDK** — the scaffolded projects are ASP.NET Core Minimal API / worker projects.
- **Dapr CLI, initialized** (`dapr init`) — components run under a Dapr sidecar locally.
- **The `intropy` CLI** — provides `intropy int create` (scaffolding) and `intropy skills add` (installs agent skills from `harbor.intropy.io/skills/<name>`).

Install the CLI via Homebrew (macOS) or the install script (macOS / Linux; Windows via WSL 2):

```bash
brew tap integrio-intropy/tap
brew trust --tap integrio-intropy/tap
brew install intropy
```

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

Verify the CLI is on your PATH before continuing:

```bash
intropy --help
```

| Blueprint | What it scaffolds |
|---|---|
| `hello-world` | Minimal ASP.NET Minimal API with a Dapr pub/sub trigger and a transactional send pipeline. `POST /publish` publishes an order; a subscribed endpoint runs it through Deserialize → Validate → Transform → Serialize → Send. Best first project. |
| `transactional` | A .NET transactional integration job: polls a local inbound folder via a Dapr binding, publishes through in-memory pub/sub, runs a full VETER send pipeline, writes the transformed result to an outbound folder. Takes an extra `empty` boolean parameter — when `true`, pipeline step bodies throw `NotImplementedException` so an agent can fill them in. |

Both blueprints take a required `name` parameter: a **PascalCase** identifier used for the .NET project, root namespace, and assembly. Dot-separated segments are allowed for nested namespaces (`MyApi`, `Int1055.OrderSync`). The blueprint derives a kebab-case `appId` from it for Dapr (e.g. `Int1055.OrderSync` → `int1055-ordersync`).

   name: HelloWorld

   ```

- No flag → the latest blueprint release.
- `--version v0.2.1` → that release tag.
- `--version main` → the default branch (useful before a release exists).

# Getting started with Intropy

This skill covers exactly one journey: from nothing to a running Intropy integration component — first scaffold, first build, first message. If a project already exists, stop and use the feature-work skills instead (see the SKIP list in the description).

An **Intropy blueprint** is a scaffold-style template: a manifest (`template.yaml`) declaring parameters, plus a skeleton file tree. The `intropy` CLI renders a blueprint plus your parameter values into a working project. Blueprints are fetched by release tag from the blueprint library, so the same inputs always produce the same output.

## Prerequisites

- **.NET 10 SDK** — the scaffolded projects are ASP.NET Core Minimal API / worker projects.
- **Dapr CLI, initialized** (`dapr init`) — components run under a Dapr sidecar locally.
- **The `intropy` CLI** — provides `intropy int create` (scaffolding) and `intropy skills add` (installs agent skills from `harbor.intropy.io/skills/<name>`).

Install the CLI via Homebrew (macOS) or the install script (macOS / Linux; Windows via WSL 2):

```bash
brew tap integrio-intropy/tap
brew trust --tap integrio-intropy/tap
brew install intropy
```

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

Verify the CLI is on your PATH before continuing:

```bash
intropy --help
```

## Available blueprints

| Blueprint | What it scaffolds |
|---|---|
| `hello-world` | Minimal ASP.NET Minimal API with a Dapr pub/sub trigger and a transactional send pipeline. `POST /publish` publishes an order; a subscribed endpoint runs it through Deserialize → Validate → Transform → Serialize → Send. Best first project. |
| `transactional` | A .NET transactional integration job: polls a local inbound folder via a Dapr binding, publishes through in-memory pub/sub, runs a full VETER send pipeline, writes the transformed result to an outbound folder. Takes an extra `empty` boolean parameter — when `true`, pipeline step bodies throw `NotImplementedException` so an agent can fill them in. |

Both blueprints take a required `name` parameter: a **PascalCase** identifier used for the .NET project, root namespace, and assembly. Dot-separated segments are allowed for nested namespaces (`MyApi`, `Int1055.OrderSync`). The blueprint derives a kebab-case `appId` from it for Dapr (e.g. `Int1055.OrderSync` → `int1055-ordersync`).

## Scaffold

1. Write a values file with the parameter values:

   ```yaml
   # values.yaml
   name: HelloWorld
   ```

2. Render the blueprint into an output directory:

   ```bash
   intropy int create hello-world -o ./hello-world -f values.yaml
   ```

Version selection:

- No flag → the latest blueprint release.
- `--version v0.2.1` → that release tag.
- `--version main` → the default branch (useful before a release exists).

Parameter values are validated against the blueprint's JSON Schema — a lowercase `name` fails the render with a pattern error rather than producing a broken project.

## What you get

A rendered `hello-world` project looks like this:

```
hello-world/
├── agent.md                     # agent-facing project guide (run command lives here)
├── README.md                    # human run instructions
├── local/
│   └── dapr-components/         # local Dapr component YAMLs
│       ├── pubsub.yaml          # in-memory pub/sub component
│       └── local-storage.yaml   # local file binding
└── src/
    ├── HelloWorld.csproj
    ├── HelloWorld.http          # sample requests for the first run
    ├── Program.cs               # DI wiring + framework + pipeline registration
    ├── appsettings*.json
    ├── Configuration/
    │   └── Constants.cs         # component/topic/binding names
    ├── Ingest/
    │   └── Endpoints.cs         # /publish + subscribed endpoint
    ├── Model/                   # OrderIn / OrderOut records
    └── Process/
        ├── OrderSendPipeline.cs
        ├── OrderSendPipelineBuilder.cs
        ├── ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs
        └── Steps/               # one file per pipeline step
```

The `transactional` blueprint follows the same shape and additionally ships an `intropy.yaml` run manifest at the root (the `spec.run` block: `appId`, `daprHttpPort`, `resourcesPath`, run command), a `Taskfile.yml`, and `local/sample-data/` with a sample order to drop in the inbound folder.

The rendered `README.md` and `agent.md` are per-project and authoritative — they carry the exact run command with the right `appId` and ports for what you scaffolded.

## First run

From the project root:

1. **Build:**

   ```bash
   dotnet build ./src
   ```

2. **Run under Dapr.** Use the run command from the project's `intropy.yaml` (when present) or `agent.md` / `README.md`. For `hello-world` it is:

   ```bash
   dapr run \
     --app-id hello-world \
     --app-port 5001 \
     --dapr-http-port 3500 \
     --resources-path ./local/dapr-components \
     -- dotnet run --project ./src --urls http://localhost:5001
   ```

3. **Publish a sample message.** Open `src/<Name>.http` and send the `POST /publish` request (from an editor with .http support, or copy it into curl):

   ```http
   POST http://localhost:5001/publish
   Content-Type: application/json

   {
     "orderId": "ORD-1001",
     "customerId": "CUST-42",
     "amount": 39.90
   }
   ```

   Dapr delivers the published message to the subscribed endpoint, which runs it through the send pipeline. The `.http` file also has a `GET /dapr/subscribe` request to inspect the discovered subscriptions.

For `transactional`, the first run is file-driven instead: create the inbound/outbound folders and copy `local/sample-data/sample-order.json` into the inbound folder as described in the rendered `README.md`; the job picks it up, processes it, and writes the transformed JSON to the outbound folder.

## Where to go next

Once the component runs, this skill's job is done. Feature work — new pipeline steps, enrichment lookups, endpoints, Dapr components, manifest changes — is covered by the sibling skills: `intropy-pipeline`, `intropy-blocks`, `intropy-endpoint`, `intropy-dapr`, and `intropy-manifest`.
